To address these limitations, we propose a federated learning approach that enables the development of robust, high-performance deep learning models for histopathology image analysis. By leveraging a decentralized architecture, our method allows for the aggregation of data from multiple institutions, reducing the need for data sharing and enabling the creation of comprehensive datasets. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by training a deep learning model for tumor detection on a dataset comprising 10,000 images from 10 different institutions, achieving a high accuracy of 0.95. Furthermore, our method is capable of handling large-scale datasets, as evidenced by our experiments on a dataset of 100,000 images from 20 institutions, where we achieved a tumor detection accuracy of 0.92. Our approach is particularly beneficial for developing deep learning models for rare diseases, where comprehensive datasets are scarce. We also investigate the impact of federated learning on the performance of deep learning models, finding that it can lead to significant improvements in accuracy, particularly when the data is highly heterogeneous. Our model, dubbed the Dilated Recurrent Temporal Convolutional Network (DRTCN), leverages time-dilated convolution to process long sequences while incorporating recurrent connections to capture local patterns. The DRTCN model is particularly effective for time-series classification tasks, as demonstrated by its performance in the MIMOSE dataset, where it achieves a classification accuracy of 96.5%. Furthermore, our model's efficiency is showcased through its ability to classify sequences of varying lengths with minimal performance degradation. Geosteering is a critical technology used in offshore drilling to ensure that wells are drilled within the desired reservoir zones. To optimize this process, real-time data from downhole sensors is analyzed to make informed decisions. However, the high cost of offshore drilling operations necessitates the development of advanced geosteering techniques that can accurately predict the position of the wellbore in real-time. This paper presents a novel approach to geosteering that leverages a combination of machine learning and physics-based modeling to enhance the accuracy of well placement predictions. The proposed method utilizes a physics-based model to simulate the behavior of the wellbore in real-time, while a machine learning algorithm is employed to optimize the model parameters and improve the accuracy of the predictions. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through a case study involving a real-world offshore drilling scenario. The results show that the proposed method can achieve a high degree of accuracy in predicting the wellbore position, with a mean absolute error of less than 1 meter. The proposed approach has the potential to significantly improve the accuracy of well placement predictions in offshore drilling operations. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing, where the goal is to identify and categorize named entities within text. Traditional NER models focus on individual entities, whereas real-world applications involve nested entities, where one entity is part of another. To address this limitation, we propose a holistic structure for modeling nested entities, which we term "nested named entity structure" (NNES). This structure allows us to leverage the relationships between nested entities and their components, enhancing the performance of NER models. To facilitate the development of holistic NER models, we introduce a novel dataset, called "nested named entity dataset" (NNED), which contains labeled data for nested entities across multiple domains. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we design a holistic NER model, called "nested named entity model" (NNEM), which utilizes the proposed structure and dataset to achieve state-of-the-art performance on the NNED dataset. Our results show that our holistic approach outperforms traditional NER models, and we make our dataset and model publicly available for further research and development. Our work aims to advance the field of NER by addressing the limitations of traditional models and providing a holistic approach to modeling nested entities. Neural machine translation has seen significant advancements in recent years, 
yet it still struggles with maintaining consistency in repetitive content. 
This issue arises from the fact that neural machine translation models are 
trained independently for each sentence, without considering the context 
of previous translations. To address this limitation, we propose a novel 
approach called Translation Memory, which utilizes a monolingual corpus to 
improve the consistency of neural machine translation. By leveraging the 
monolingual corpus, we can create a translation memory that captures the 
repetitive patterns in the data, enabling the model to draw upon this 
knowledge to enhance the consistency of its translations. We demonstrate 
the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on the WMT 2014 
English-to-German task, achieving a significant improvement of 1.1 BLEU 
points over the baseline model. Furthermore, we show that our approach 
can be applied to other tasks, including neural machine translation with 
domain adaptation. Our code and pre-trained models are available at 
https://github.com/zhengyifeng/translation-memory.

Cross-domain recommendation has been extensively researched to enhance user experience by leveraging information from multiple domains. However, most existing methods are limited to a single sparse domain, neglecting the potential benefits of incorporating multiple sparse domains. To address this limitation, we propose a novel Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) framework that effectively utilizes information from multiple sparse domains. By integrating a novel multi-sparse domain attention mechanism, MSDCR effectively captures the underlying relationships between user and item interactions across multiple domains. Furthermore, MSDCR incorporates a novel multi-sparse domain graph attention mechanism to model the complex connections between users and items within each domain. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art cross-domain recommendation methods. Additionally, we conduct comprehensive ablation studies to validate the efficacy of the proposed multi-sparse domain attention and graph attention mechanisms. The code for MSDCR is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyuanliu/MSDCR.

Reinforcement learning agents often rely on experience replay to improve their performance, but this approach has a significant drawback: it assumes that past experiences are equally valuable for training. In reality, the value of experiences can vary greatly, and using a uniform sampling method can lead to inefficient training. To address this issue, we propose a novel experience replay method called Adaptive Experience Replay (AER), which selectively samples experiences based on their estimated value. AER uses a secondary neural network to evaluate the value of experiences and adaptively adjusts the sampling probability to prioritize high-value experiences. We demonstrate the effectiveness of AER through experiments on various continuous control tasks, showing that it outperforms traditional experience replay methods and achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods. Notably, AER's adaptive sampling strategy leads to faster learning and improved performance, and we provide theoretical insights into its benefits. We also introduce a new algorithm called Adaptive Experience Replay with Prioritized Sampling (AER-PS), which further enhances AER's performance by incorporating prioritized experience replay. AER-PS achieves state-of-the-art performance on several continuous control tasks, and we make our code publicly available for reproducibility.

Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success in detecting large-scale objects, but they often struggle with identifying objects that span multiple grid cells in the feature pyramid network (FPN). This challenge arises because FPN's hierarchical structure leads to a significant decrease in spatial resolution as it progresses, resulting in a substantial loss of object information. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel object detection framework called the Hierarchical Feature Pyramid Network (HFPN), which incorporates a hierarchical structure that preserves object information across the feature pyramid. By utilizing a hierarchical structure, HFPN can effectively capture objects of varying sizes and reduce the impact of the spatial resolution loss in FPN. We demonstrate the effectiveness of HFPN through experiments on the COCO dataset, achieving state-of-the-art performance in object detection and surpassing the performance of FPN-based methods. Additionally, we showcase the versatility of HFPN by adapting it for instance segmentation and achieving competitive results. In contrast, our study introduces a novel defense framework centered on improving the discriminator's adversarial resistance. By leveraging a robust discriminator, we can effectively counteract the impact of adversarial attacks on the generator. Our framework is versatile, accommodating a range of generator architectures, including cGANs, and can be seamlessly integrated into existing defense methods. Experimental evaluations on multiple datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, showcasing improved robustness and accuracy in the presence of adversarial attacks. Furthermore, our findings suggest that quasiperiodic modulation can be leveraged to enhance light localization in certain configurations, and we propose a method to optimize the quasiperiodic structure for maximum localization. Our research provides valuable insights into the complex interplay between disorder and quasiperiodicity in photonic quasicrystals, and our results have implications for the design of photonic devices that utilize quasiperiodic structures. Additionally, our study highlights the potential for quasiperiodic modulation to control light localization, and we anticipate that our findings will contribute to the development of novel photonic devices and applications. Knowledge distillation is a well-established technique for training efficient neural networks by leveraging the knowledge of a more complex and accurate model. Despite its effectiveness, the process is typically resource-intensive due to the need for multiple forward passes through the teacher network. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach called "distillation through residual connections" that enables efficient knowledge distillation by utilizing the residual connections within the student network. By leveraging the residual connections, we can distill knowledge from the teacher network with minimal additional computation, thereby reducing the overall computational cost. Our approach is particularly beneficial for large-scale neural networks, where the teacher network's computational cost is prohibitively expensive. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, showcasing comparable performance to traditional knowledge distillation methods while achieving a significant reduction in computational cost. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyuanliu/ResDistill.

We demonstrate the efficacy of our framework through experiments on imitation learning tasks, showcasing its ability to effectively utilize suboptimal data and outperform existing methods. Our approach is particularly beneficial in scenarios where high-quality demonstrations are scarce, and we provide a theoretical analysis of its performance. Furthermore, HyperPrompt's hypernetwork can be optimized to produce high-quality prompts, thereby enhancing the performance of the underlying language model. Our experiments demonstrate that HyperPrompt excels in few-shot learning settings, achieving superior results compared to conventional prompt-based methods. The anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials is characterized by the generation of a transverse voltage in response to an applied current, and it has been extensively studied in various materials, including ferromagnetic metals, semiconductors, and insulators. In recent years, significant research has focused on the anomalous Hall effect in transition metal phosphides, particularly in Co2P and NiP, which exhibit high anomalous Hall conductivity. This review aims to provide an in-depth examination of the anomalous Hall effect in transition metal phosphides, covering the underlying physics, experimental findings, and theoretical models. We also discuss the potential applications of these materials in spintronics and the challenges that need to be addressed in future research. Furthermore, we highlight the importance of considering the crystal structure and electronic properties of transition metal phosphides in understanding the anomalous Hall effect. Lastly, we discuss the potential of these materials in achieving high anomalous Hall conductivity and the need for further investigation into their properties. This review is intended to serve as a comprehensive resource for researchers interested in the anomalous Hall effect in transition metal phosphides.

Knowledge distillation has emerged as a valuable technique for enhancing the performance of ranking models by leveraging the expertise of more accurate but computationally expensive models. Despite its effectiveness, knowledge distillation is often hindered by the need for large-scale training data, which can be costly to obtain. In this study, we explore the potential of knowledge distillation to improve ranking models using limited data. We introduce a novel distillation method that utilizes a compact and efficient model to extract relevant information from a large-scale dataset, which is then used to train a smaller model on a limited dataset. Our approach, known as "knowledge distillation from a large-scale dataset" (KDL), is particularly effective when training data is scarce. We demonstrate the efficacy of KDL through experiments on two benchmark datasets, where we achieve significant improvements in ranking performance using limited data. Our results show that KDL outperforms traditional knowledge distillation methods and achieves comparable performance to training from scratch on large-scale datasets. We also examine the impact of KDL on different model architectures and provide insights into the optimal choice of hyperparameters. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyuanliu/kdl.

Furthermore, we explore the relationship between the annealing time and the accuracy of the results, and find that the optimal annealing time is inversely proportional to the strength of the interactions. This issue is particularly pronounced in multi-organ segmentation tasks, where annotating each pixel accurately can be extremely time-consuming. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach that utilizes weak annotations, specifically organ-level masks, to segment multiple organs simultaneously. This approach leverages a dual-task framework, where a segmentation task and a classification task are performed in parallel. The segmentation task aims to segment the entire image, while the classification task focuses on identifying the presence or absence of specific organs within the image. By incorporating a classification loss, the model is trained to recognize organ-specific features, which enhances its ability to segment multiple organs accurately. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach on the LiTS dataset, achieving state-of-the-art results in segmenting multiple organs with limited annotations. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyuanliu/weak-supervision-multi-organ-segmentation.

Our research provides a scalable and efficient solution for cross-device federated learning, paving the way for the development of more complex hierarchical structures and the exploration of new optimization techniques. A key challenge in UDA is the issue of domain shift, which arises from the difference in data distributions between source and target domains. By leveraging these synthetic domains, we can adapt to the target domain through a process of domain alignment. Our approach is particularly effective when combined with adversarial training, which enables the model to learn a common representation across domains. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through experiments on image classification tasks, achieving state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks, including Office-Home, Office-31, and VisDA-2017. This approach is particularly effective when trained on limited data, such as small annotated regions within a larger image. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through experiments on the CAMELYON16 dataset, achieving state-of-the-art results with a significant reduction in annotation time. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyuan-yu/weakly-supervised-nucleus-segmentation.

Reinforcement learning is a widely used technique for training agents to achieve complex goals in dynamic environments. However, its effectiveness can be hindered by external factors such as state variables and rewards that are not under the agent's control. These external influences can be detrimental to the agent's performance, causing it to become stuck in suboptimal policies. In this research, we introduce a novel approach to address this issue by incorporating an auxiliary control objective that is designed to counteract the negative effects of external factors. This auxiliary control is achieved through a separate reinforcement learning process that operates in parallel to the primary goal-oriented learning. By leveraging the benefits of multi-task learning, we demonstrate that our approach can significantly enhance the agent's performance and policy stability. Our method is particularly effective in scenarios where the external influences are dynamic and unpredictable, and we provide a theoretical analysis of its benefits. We also present experimental results that showcase the efficacy of our approach in various environments, including those with time-varying rewards and state variables. Our findings indicate that our method can lead to substantial improvements in policy stability and performance, and we provide a comprehensive analysis of the factors that contribute to these gains. Our research offers a new perspective on reinforcement learning, highlighting the importance of considering external factors and the benefits of multi-task learning in complex environments. Video super-resolution is a challenging task due to the presence of complex temporal dynamics and varying frame rates. Current state-of-the-art methods primarily focus on single-frame processing, neglecting the inherent temporal coherence and grid structure of video data. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel video super-resolution framework that incorporates second-order grid propagation and flow-guided deformable alignment. By leveraging a grid-based propagation module, our model effectively captures the temporal evolution of video data. Additionally, a deformable alignment module is employed to align frames with varying frame rates, enabling the model to handle temporal misalignment. Our proposed framework, dubbed GridSR, is capable of handling videos with diverse frame rates and temporal dynamics, resulting in a significant improvement in video super-resolution performance. Experimental evaluations on various datasets demonstrate GridSR's superiority over existing methods, with notable improvements in PSNR and SSIM scores. The code for GridSR is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyuanliu/GridSR.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, agents are trained on a variety of tasks to leverage the benefits of shared knowledge and skills. By learning across multiple objectives, the agent can develop a more comprehensive understanding of the environment, enabling it to excel in each individual task. However, the agent's performance is often hindered by the conflicting goals of the tasks, which can lead to a trade-off between exploration and exploitation. In this research, we explore the concept of multi-task reinforcement learning with a twist: the agent is trained on a set of tasks that are not directly related to the primary objective. Instead, the agent must learn to navigate a meta-environment that contains a hidden reward structure, which is only revealed through the agent's interactions with the secondary tasks. This setup creates a unique challenge for the agent, as it must balance exploration and exploitation across multiple tasks to uncover the underlying reward structure. We propose a novel algorithm, Meta-Task Reinforcement Learning (Meta-TRL), which utilizes a hierarchical representation of the meta-environment to guide the agent's exploration and learning. By leveraging the structure of the meta-environment, Meta-TRL enables the agent to efficiently explore the environment and discover the underlying reward structure, ultimately leading to improved performance on the primary task. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Meta-TRL through a series of experiments, showcasing its ability to excel in complex environments with hidden reward structures. Additionally, we provide a theoretical analysis of Meta-TRL's performance, highlighting its advantages over traditional reinforcement learning algorithms. Our findings indicate that Meta-TRL can achieve superior performance by leveraging the structure of the meta-environment, and we discuss the implications of our research for the field of multi-task reinforcement learning. We also introduce a new benchmark, Meta-Task Reinforcement Learning (Meta-TRL-Bench), which provides a comprehensive evaluation framework for assessing the performance of meta-task reinforcement learning algorithms. We believe that our research and benchmark will contribute to the advancement of meta-task reinforcement learning, enabling the development of more efficient and effective algorithms for complex reinforcement learning tasks. We have made our code and data available at https://github.com/andrewliao21/MetaTRL. We have also made our Meta-TRL-Bench benchmark available at https://github.com/andrewliao21/MetaTRL-Bench. We also examine the impact of temperature on tunneling conductance, finding that the peak's width is directly proportional to the nanowire's temperature. Furthermore, we demonstrate that tunneling conductance can be described by a universal function that depends on the ratio of the nanowire's temperature to the superconducting gap. Our results provide a theoretical framework for understanding tunneling conductance in topological superconducting nanowires. Additionally, we discuss the potential for tunneling spectroscopy to detect Majorana modes and the challenges associated with this approach. Our findings are relevant to ongoing and future experiments on topological superconducting nanowires.

A key challenge in audio-visual source localization is identifying the source of sounds in videos. Current methods rely on supervised learning and are limited by the quality of their training data. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called Hard Sample Mining for Source Localization (HMSL). HMSL introduces a new loss function that selectively focuses on misclassified samples during training, effectively leveraging unlabeled data to improve source localization performance. By incorporating a confidence-based sampling strategy, HMSL prioritizes the most uncertain predictions, allowing it to effectively utilize unlabeled data to refine its predictions. Experimental results demonstrate that HMSL achieves state-of-the-art performance on the SoundSource dataset, outperforming existing methods by a significant margin. Additionally, our approach excels in unsupervised settings, showcasing its ability to learn from unlabeled data. The code for HMSL is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyuanliu/HMSL.

Participants were presented with a series of choices between immediate and delayed rewards, with the added complexity of having to wait for the delayed reward. The findings suggest that impulsivity is closely tied to delay discounting, and that the value of rewards is influenced by the time it takes to receive them.
